Series / 8 parts

From policy to action: the last mile of robotics control

Part 1October 2, 202636 min read

One equation, and every way the arm misses it

Start from torque = inertia × acceleration, then add each term a cheap servo arm really has: gravity, friction, a payload, dead time, a dead band. Each term is one way the arm misses its target.

↗Part 2October 3, 202614 min read

Seeing finer than the sensor

The sensor side of the joint equation: why differences of encoder ticks explode the noise, and how an observer or a Kalman filter can estimate an angle finer than one tick.

↗Part 3October 4, 202629 min read

Six ways to choose the goal

One general formula for the goal sent to a servo. Every controller I built, from a plain look-ahead to MPC, is that formula with some terms set to zero.

↗Part 4October 5, 202619 min read

Learning what the physics misses

Where a neural network fits in a robot controller. A network that learns only what the physics model gets wrong does the same job as a Kalman disturbance estimate, with more freedom, and this is where recent research is going.

↗Part 5 · HardwareOctober 5, 202617 min read

A pen holder that shows the arm’s error, not its own

I want to see my SO-101 trajectory errors as ink on paper. For that, the pen must not add an error of its own. I made five holder designs. The one I release is a printed sleeve that slides onto the stock gripper: 4 printed parts, nothing to buy, any pen from 8 to 13 mm.

↗Part 6October 11, 202625 min read

Where the last millimeter of my drawing arm goes

My SO-101 arm cannot see its own pen tip. A tablet can. Here is what the tablet showed: how much error a learned correction removes, which causes are left, and why the base joint matters most.

↗Part 7October 15, 202611 min read

Teaching my drawing arm to keep learning

After part 6: direct motor drive, learning between drawings, feedback during a stroke, and a twin tested across days. The repeat floor is not a claim of one-millimeter control.

↗Part 8October 15, 202613 min read

How do I get the XYZ position of my robot's tool tip?

A drawing tablet measures a pen in a plane. Cameras, marker tracking, and laser trackers extend the view into space, with different costs and sources of error.
